The {{nihongo|'''Inaridai Kofun Group'''|稲荷台古墳群}} is a {{ill|Kofun cluster|ja|古墳群}} or a group of [[Kofun]] located in the [[Chiba Prefecture]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |date=1952 |title=Review of The Prehistory of Japan |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3248573 |journal=Artibus Asiae |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=288–292 |doi=10.2307/3248573 |issn=0004-3648|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Findings ==
The cluster includes Inaridai Kofun No. 1 Kofun, from which the [[Inaridai Sword]] was taken from.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pearson |first=Richard |date=1990 |title=Review of Protohistoric Yamato: Archaeology of the First Japanese State |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2719219 |journal=Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=768–775 |doi=10.2307/2719219 |issn=0073-0548|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Some of the earliest pottery in the [[Kantō region]] has been found in this Kofun, giving the kofun its name.<ref name=":0" />

== Location ==
Located on the west of the [[Bōsō Peninsula]] and just east of [[Tokyo]], Inaridai is part of a concentration of early archaeological sites, which also includes [[Shakujii, Tokyo|Shakujii]], in [[Tokyo]]'s [[Nerima, Tokyo|Nerima ward]], among others. Northeast of these locations are the later sites, categorized as Proto-Jomon. These Proto-Jomon sites are distinguished by pottery that predominantly features fiber or cord impressions.<ref name=":1" />

In the Miura Peninsula, pottery has shell marks. In the Western Kanto Plain, pottery changed from fiber marks to cord marks. Inaridai is a key site in this change.<ref name=":1" />

== Usage in periodization ==
The Kofun cluster gives its name to Inaridai pottery, the oldest pottery type in the [[Kantō region]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kidder |first=J. Edward |date=1954 |title=A Reconsideration of the "Pre-Pottery" Culture of Japan |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3249085 |journal=Artibus Asiae |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=135–143 |doi=10.2307/3249085 |issn=0004-3648|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The Inaridai No. 1 Kofun and the Inaridai Kofun group are found in the Kanto loam layer. This layer contains both early [[Jōmon pottery|Jomon pottery]] types, such as Inaridai, Haijima, and Tado I, as well as other artifacts.<ref name=":0" /> It is also used to categorize figurines.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maringer |first=J. |last2=Kidder |first2=J. Edward |date=1957 |title=Review of The Jomon Pottery of Japan, J. Edward Kidder, Jr. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3249384 |journal=Artibus Asiae |volume=20 |issue=2/3 |pages=206–207 |doi=10.2307/3249384 |issn=0004-3648|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and other implements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Yampolsky |first=Philip |date=1951 |title=Review of Historical Studies in Japan, 1949. |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2049017 |journal=The Far Eastern Quarterly |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=392–396 |doi=10.2307/2049017 |issn=0363-6917|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tamburello |first=Adolfo |date=1962 |title=Review of Japan Before Buddhism Italian edition: II Giappone prima del Buddhismo |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/29754663 |journal=East and West |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=377–383 |issn=0012-8376}}</ref>

In the Kanto valley of Japan, the Inaridai is one of the oldest pottery found. It has a special rolling marking on it. Experts aren't sure where this marking method came from. Wu{{Who|date=November 2023}} thinks it might have started as a useful feature before becoming just for decoration. The Inaridai pottery dates back to just after the start of the proto-Jomon period. This makes it important for studying early [[Japanese pottery and porcelain|Japanese pottery]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tolstoy |first=Paul |date=1953 |title=Some Amerasian Pottery Traits in North Asian Prehistory |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/276410 |journal=American Antiquity |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=25–39 |doi=10.2307/276410 |issn=0002-7316|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
